The storm knocked out the power at Nani's house, and the torch was missing. Ira lay stiff under the quilt. Lightning flashed. A tall figure stood in the corner with long arms.
"Didi," she whispered. "There's a monster."
Aadhya didi fumbled for her phone and switched on its light. "Where?"
Ira pointed. The light showed Nana's raincoat hanging on the hook, its sleeves dangling.
"Touch it," said Aadhya. Ira crept over and squeezed a wet sleeve. "It's just the raincoat."
She climbed back and let Aadhya hug her until the thunder faded.

qa.q: What was hanging on the hook?
qa.a: Nana's raincoat.

qa.q: What was Ira feeling when she lay stiff under the quilt?
qa.a: Ira was frightened; in the dark the raincoat looked like a monster to her.

qa.q: Which step helped Ira tell imagination from reality?
qa.a: Aadhya let Ira see and touch the raincoat herself, so Ira found out it was not a monster.

qa.q: How might Aadhya feel during the storm?
qa.a: Aadhya may feel a bit tense herself with no power, but she stays calm to comfort Ira.

grounding: During a power cut a child checks a scary shape, finds it is a raincoat, and accepts a hug.

On a foggy December night in Delhi, Seema screamed. "Mumma! Something white is at the window!"
Himani came in and sat on the bed. "Show me."
Seema pointed at a pale shape floating outside, moving in the wind.
"Shall we look together?" Himani held her hand and drew the curtain back. It was Mrs Bedi's white shawl, drying on the next balcony.
Seema stared. "It looked like a ghost."
"In the dark, lots of things do."
Seema let Himani tuck her in, holding her hand a little longer.

qa.q: What was the white shape at the window?
qa.a: Mrs Bedi's white shawl, drying on the next balcony.

qa.q: What was Seema feeling when she said "It looked like a ghost"?
qa.a: Seema was still a little shaken but relieved to see it was only a shawl.

qa.q: What did Himani do that helped Seema?
qa.a: Himani didn't laugh; she looked together with Seema, so Seema could check the scary shape herself.

qa.q: What would change if Himani had said "Don't be silly, go to sleep"?
qa.a: Seema would probably stay scared and feel dismissed, without finding out what the shape really was.

grounding: On a foggy winter night a mother helps her child see that a scary shape is a shawl.

"Mumma, there's a monster under my bed. It growls."
Binita put down the lamp. "Growls? Like what?"
"Grrr, grrrr."
They listened. Rain drummed on the tin roof. The drainpipe gurgled. Grrr, grrrr.
"Hmm," said Binita. "What does the drainpipe sound like when it rains?"
Sahil listened again. "…Like that."
"Want to look under the bed with me?"
Sahil peeked with the lamp. Dust and one lost sock. "No monster."
"No monster. But you can still hold my hand."
Sahil held it and yawned.

qa.q: What did Sahil find under the bed?
qa.a: Dust and one lost sock.

qa.q: What was Sahil feeling when he said the monster growls?
qa.a: Sahil was scared, because the drainpipe sound in the rain seemed like a growl to him.

qa.q: How did Binita help Sahil work it out himself?
qa.a: She asked what the drainpipe sounds like in rain and let him look under the bed, so he could see there was no monster.

qa.q: How might Binita feel when Sahil yawns and holds her hand?
qa.a: Binita probably feels relieved and tender 🤍, glad he is calm enough to sleep.

grounding: On a rainy night a child tests his fear of a growling monster and accepts comfort.

"Don't squash it!" said Karthik.
"Why? It's yucky."

qa.q: How does Karthik see the worm?

The science quiz in Toronto was on Friday, and Kofi's head felt like a leaky bucket.
"I read the chapter three times," he told Bao at lunch. "Nothing stayed."
Bao pulled out a stack of small cards. "Reading isn't enough. Write the question on one side, answer on the other. Then test yourself."
They made twenty cards. For the planets, Bao taught him a silly sentence: "My Very Eager Mother Just Served Us Noodles."
Kofi laughed. "That's ridiculous."
"That's why you'll remember it."
They tested each other that day, then again on Wednesday. On Friday, Kofi wrote all eight planets in order without stopping.

qa.q: What was Kofi feeling when he said nothing stayed?
qa.a: Kofi felt frustrated and worried, because reading three times hadn't helped him remember.

qa.q: Which methods helped Kofi, and why?

The panchayat was deciding whether to turn the old store-room at the village school into a library. The teacher asked each child to write a paragraph: yes or no, and why.
Madhav wrote: "Yes. Library is good." Then he stopped.
Lokesh leaned over. "That's one line. Why is it good?"

In Dublin, Liam's homework was to write an opinion paragraph. He chose "Dogs are better than cats."
His sister Nadia, who had a cat, read it. "You just wrote 'Dogs are the best' five times."
Liam scowled. "Because they are."
"Then prove it. Give reasons."
Liam thought. "Okay. One, dogs come for walks with you. Two, they can help people, like guide dogs. Three, they're happy when you come home."
"Better," said Nadia. "Still wrong, but better."
Liam wrote the three reasons, each with an example, and finished: "So I think dogs make better pets."

qa.q: What did Liam write five times at first?
qa.a: "Dogs are the best."

qa.q: What was Liam feeling when he scowled?
qa.a: Liam felt annoyed and defensive when Nadia criticised his paragraph.

qa.q: What made Liam's paragraph stronger?
qa.a: He gave three reasons, each with an example, and ended with a clear opinion sentence.

qa.q: How does Nadia see Liam's paragraph by the end?
qa.a: Nadia still disagrees with his opinion, but she thinks his writing is better because it has reasons.

grounding: A child in Ireland learns to back up an opinion with reasons.

Sit, Asif. You asked why I speak so many languages. Let me tell you.
When I was your age in Pune, at home we spoke Marathi. In the market, Hindi. And my father sent me to an English school, where the teacher scolded me for saying "aai" instead of "mother".
One day my friend's grandmother came from Hyderabad. She spoke only Urdu. Nobody could talk to her. I remembered some Urdu from the tailor next door, and I helped her buy vegetables.
She held my face and blessed me. That day I stopped feeling that mixing languages was wrong. I was Yash who could talk to everybody.

qa.q: How might the friend's grandmother have felt when young Yash spoke to her in Urdu?
qa.a: She probably felt relieved and grateful to finally be understood in a strange city.

grounding: An elder tells a child how he learned to use different languages for home, market, school and others.

The clerk said in English, "Please fill this form with PAN details."
Paati looked at Devika, lost.
Devika leaned in. "Paati, avaru form-la ungalu PAN number ezhudha sollraaru." Then to the clerk: "She doesn't have it with her. Can she bring it tomorrow?"

In Kraków, Marek and his friend Tariq filled the kitchen sink with water.
"Predictions," said Marek, grabbing a pencil. "The apple will sink. It's heavy."
Tariq thought. "The key will float. It's small."
They dropped them in. The apple bobbed on top. The key dropped straight down.
Marek stared. "Wrong. Both of us."
"Write it down anyway," said Tariq. "What we guessed, and what happened."
Marek wrote. Then: "So small doesn't mean float. Let's try a coin and a cork."

qa.q: What happened to the key?
qa.a: The key dropped straight down.

qa.q: What was Marek feeling when he stared at the apple floating?
qa.a: Marek felt surprised and puzzled, because it didn't do what he had predicted.

qa.q: Which habits of a good scientist did Marek and Tariq show?
qa.a: They wrote down their guesses and what really happened, then planned new tests instead of ignoring the surprise.

qa.q: How does Tariq see being wrong?
qa.a: Tariq sees it as part of the experiment, worth writing down, not something to hide.

grounding: Two children in Poland test predictions about floating and sinking and record the results.

In the school science lab, Ritu and Keerthana each had an ice cube on a plate.
"Salt will make it melt faster," said Ritu.
"No, slower. Salt is dry," said Keerthana.
They sprinkled salt on one cube and left the other plain. They wrote their guesses on the board and watched the clock.
After ten minutes, the salted cube was a puddle with a small lump left. The plain one was still mostly there.
Keerthana crossed out her guess. "I was wrong."
"Why does salt do that?" Ritu asked.
They went to find the teacher together.

qa.q: How long did they watch before checking the cubes?
qa.a: Ten minutes.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling when she crossed out her guess?
qa.a: Keerthana may have felt a little disappointed, but she was honest about being wrong.

qa.q: What could Ritu and Keerthana do next to learn more?
qa.a: They could try the test again, maybe with sugar too, and ask the teacher why salt speeds up melting.

qa.q: How might Ritu feel about her prediction being right?
qa.a: Ritu likely feels pleased, but more curious than proud, since she immediately asks why.

grounding: Two children test a prediction about salt and ice and accept what actually happens.
